items.title: Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
items.summary: This post announces native PyTorch backends for vLLM and SGLang powered by TorchTPU, enabling developers to run and optimize serving workloads using familiar PyTorch tools. Built in collaboration with open-source project maintainers, these engines include optimized TPU kernel implementations, production-ready features like KV cache management with TPU Sync, and disaggregated serving. Public benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and industry-leading cost efficiency on Ironwood TPU across long-context and agentic workloads.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
items.summary: Google Workspace now offers native support for Markdown (.md) files, allowing developers and AI agents to seamlessly collaborate on documentation directly in Google Docs without manual file conversions. This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.

items.title: Building Conversational Commerce with Multi-Agent Swarms on GCP: A Working Prototype
items.summary: This document provides a publication template and metadata structure for a technical blog post focused on building Conversational User Interfaces (CUIs) using AI. The framework helps engineers organize their guides and solutions to effectively share AI-driven conversational interface designs with the developer community.

items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
items.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

items.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
items.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. These updates require no changes to frontend renderers or component catalogs, offering flexible performance levers for generative UI development across Python, TypeScript, and Dart.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
items.summary: Google Research has completed the 32-bit open-source Coral NPU RISC-V architecture with the introduction of its Matrix Execution Unit, which delivers up to 1 TOPS while targeting 10 mW average power for edge inference. Alongside this architecture, the release of the v1.0 open-source IREE/MLIR compiler allows developers to take models from JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow straight to Coral NPU hardware without writing custom assembly. Developers can now prototype and deploy these multimodal edge applications using new hardware options like the Synaptics Astra SR200 MCU series and globally available Coralboard devkits.12

items.title: Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

It demonstrates how to catch prompt regressions, evaluate model backend swaps using side-by-side trace comparisons, and automate evaluation passes. Developers will also learn how to integrate nightly scheduled runs with threshold-based alerting to track quality over time.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Weekly Digest Delivery: Fixing Malformed Payloads in a 256KB Node.js Background Queue

items.title: React Page Missing From Google? Three Checks Before You Rewrite It
items.summary: A React page can work in your browser while its initial HTTP response contains only an app shell. That observation alone does not prove Google cannot index it. Separate three questions: what did the server return, what could Google render, and what version is currently indexed? Pick a service or article URL with a unique heading. Save its response: curl -sSL -D headers.txt -o page.html https://example.com/services/web-development Check the status, robots directives, canonical URL and main content. Compare it with the homepage. Also test a URL that should not exist: an error screen returning HTTP 200 can create a soft-404 problem. Use Search Console’s URL Inspection live test. Search the tested HTML for a sentence unique to the page. If it is absent, investigate failed scripts, data requests and content that depends on clicking a button. A loader in a screenshot is a useful clue, but inspect the HTML too. Google documents the distinction between crawling, rendering and indexing in its JavaScript SEO guide. items.summary: The easy and straightforward guide to reading scales, measuring and avoiding hidden errors that can add up to the cost of projects. Scale used in construction drawings is the relationship between the paper measurement and the actual measurement on the construction site. A scale of 1:100 means that for every 1 cm measured on a drawing, 100 cm (or 1 meter) is measured on the actual building. The first step to correct measurements, material quantities, and cost estimates is to read it correctly. Step 1: Convert drawing length to real length // scale = the "N" in 1:N. Example: 1:100 -> 100 // 4 cm on a 1:100 drawing For imperial scales, convert the notation to a ratio first: // "1/4 inch = 1 foot" -> 1:48 console.log(imperialToRatio(1 / 4, 1)); // 48 Now one function handles both systems. Step 2: The real problem is the PDF On paper, scale is reliable. On screen, it is not. A PDF has no inherent "real world" size. Zoom level, page size, and printing options all change what you measure. Worse, a PDF printed with "fit to page" no longer matches its labeled scale. A 1:100 sheet can end up near 1:120. items.title: You're Still Optimizing Re-Renders Wrong: The Vue 3 Architecture That Outsmarted the Virtual DOM
items.summary: If you have built applications in modern frontend frameworks, you have almost certainly encountered the re-render nightmare. In traditional Virtual DOM architectures, updating a single state variable often causes an entire component tree to re-execute from top to bottom. To prevent performance bottlenecks, developers must manually wrap calculations in memoization hooks, carefully manage dependency arrays, and worry about stale closures: // The manual dependency tightrope const userProfile = useMemo(() => { return calculateComplexMetrics(user, filters); }, [user.id, filters.activeStatus]); // Miss a dependency, and your UI breaks One missing dependency in that array creates subtle, agonizing bugs. One unnecessary dependency triggers expensive cascading re-renders across dozens of child components. Then you look at Vue 3: // In Vue 3: No dependency array. No manual memoization. const userProfile = computed(() => { return calculateComplexMetrics(user.value, filters.activeStatus); }); You mutate user.value.name, and only the exact paragraph rendering that name updates. items.title: A license-key server on Cloudflare Workers + KV, with signed keys and activation limits
items.summary: If you sell a desktop app, CLI, plugin or template, you eventually need license keys: one per sale, checked inside the app, and switched off on refund. Hosted services do this for roughly $29 a month. You can also run the whole thing yourself on Cloudflare Workers + KV, with no server to babysit. This post walks through the design I settled on. It is useful whether or not you use my kit (more on that at the end; I made it). Create a key (admin only) and show it once. Validate a key (public endpoint) from your app. Limit activations per machine. Revoke a key. Create keys automatically when a sale happens, and revoke on refund. That is a small surface, which suits a Worker. Generate keys from 100 bits of randomness, encoded in Crockford base32, grouped for humans: KB-7K2XM-9QF3T-0ABCD-HJ4WZ. Crockford base32 skips ambiguous letters, and you can normalize typos (treat I and L as 1, O as 0) when a user types a key in. Do not store the key. Store SHA-256(key) in KV as the record id, with the metadata next to it: product, max activations, expiry, revoked flag. If your KV leaks, nobody can use it to get working keys. items.title: A birth time is a wall clock, not an instant: how one timezone bug moves a rising sign
items.summary: If you turn "14:00 on 15 July 1990" into a Date on whatever device runs your code, you get a different instant on every device. For an astrology calculator that is not a rounding problem: the same birth data produced four different rising signs. The fix is to store the wall-clock reading together with the IANA zone of the birth place, and to convert on the server, never from the runtime's own zone. I build Burcapp, a free set of Turkish astrology calculators, and this bug is why birth time now travels through the whole app as a wall clock plus a zone. Here is the whole thing with the numbers. A birth certificate says "14:00". That is a reading on a clock at the birth place. It becomes an instant only once you know which zone that clock was in on that date. JavaScript's Date parser treats a date-time string without an offset as local time, meaning the local time of the device that runs it: const wall = new Date("1990-07-15T14:00:00"); console.log(Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone, wall.toISOString()); Running that with TZ set to four different zones: Device zone Instant (UTC) Europe/Istanbul 1990-07-15T11:00:00.000Z UTC 1990-07-15T14:00:00.000Z America/New_York 1990-0

items.title: E-commerce Node.js Background Job Queue — Create a Renewal Worker with Safe Idempotency
items.summary: A Node.js background job queue with one worker is the quickest way to delay an e-commerce renewal reminder until a business deadline; create a small queue contract first, then make the worker idempotent because delivery is at-least-once. Infrai fits this leg when you want a plain REST boundary that can be swapped without rewriting the reminder code, while RabbitMQ, BullMQ, and Temporal remain credible alternatives. Short answer: publish a compact reminder payload, consume it with one public worker, ack only after the send is durably recorded, and nack transient failures with bounded retries that end in a dead-letter queue (DLQ). Store an idempotency key before doing the side effect. The concrete job is ordinary: a merchant changes a renewal date, and the system must hold the reminder until that date rather than send it immediately. A seven-day delay is within the queue's limit. Longer work should be triggered by cron into a queue, then performed by the worker; cron itself has a 900-second execution ceiling. Start with one queue named renewal-reminders. items.title: S3-Compatible File Downloads: Node.js Presigned URLs with Reversible Retention
items.summary: Short answer: generate a short-lived presigned download URL from the storage service, keep the bucket private, and make the object key part of a documented contract rather than passing arbitrary user input through the route. For an S3-compatible storage node, use the storage object's presign operation with the bucket and key as path parameters. The response contains the URL to use before its expiration time; that second request goes to the returned URL and must not carry the storage API's Authorization header. That solves the download, but it does not solve retention by itself. A training-artifact pipeline still needs to decide which exports remain, what deletion means, and how an operator proves what happened later. My default is private objects, a database record for the retention decision, and a presigned URL only at the edge of the workflow. It is a small boundary, and it is much easier to replace than a codebase that knows a provider's internal SDK everywhere. items.title: Node.js Express Queue Worker — Token Bucket Rate Limits for 429 Webhook Backoff
items.summary: A gaming webhook worker should spend its latency budget on a token-bucket admission check, then treat HTTP 429 as a scheduled event instead of an immediate loop. Keep one idempotency key per delivery, honor Retry-After, and cap exponential backoff with jitter. That prevents duplicate match, purchase, and inventory events while recovering after a partner throttle. Short answer: use the bucket for normal traffic and a durable delayed-retry queue for rejected traffic; a retry must never bypass the queue merely because its payload is old. The worker owns four invariants. A token is consumed only when an outbound attempt is about to start. Every event keeps one stable key, such as game-8472:purchase:991, across retries. The scheduler persists the next eligible timestamp before acknowledging the queue message. The delivery ledger records the response class, attempt count, and last error code. Those invariants define the failure boundary. A crash before a ledger write can produce an at-least-once attempt, so the receiver must deduplicate. items.title: SaaS Image Thumbnails: Object Storage, CDN, or Upload Resizing with Node.js
items.summary: Short answer: for a beginner SaaS serving authenticated game reports, keep originals and generated thumbnails as separate objects, and create the thumbnail in a backend worker after upload. It is the easiest path to predictable large-file throughput. Add an image CDN only when you truly need on-the-fly, edge URL transformations. Resizing synchronously inside the upload request is the option I would avoid first. The mental model is simple: the upload request stores bytes, a worker transforms bytes, and the read path serves a known object key. That before/after split keeps a slow resize from holding an authenticated customer request open. Start with object storage. Put originals under a stable prefix such as reports/original/ and write outputs under reports/thumb/. Your database can store both keys, dimensions, and a generation status. A report page then reads a thumbnail object directly through your authenticated backend, while the original remains available for export. This is deliberately boring. items.title: Day 25/90: The fetch that "succeeded" on a 404
items.summary: Day 25/90: The fetch that "succeeded" on a 404 90 Day JavaScript Challenge: Zero to Production The bug report was short: a user's saved settings kept silently resetting. The UI said "Saved!" every time. The data was not saved. I traced it to a route rename. We had moved an endpoint, and one caller still hit the old path, so its request came back as a 404. The part that should have raised an alarm did nothing. Here is the function: async function updateProfile(profile) { const reply = await fetch("/account/profile", { method: "PUT", body: JSON.stringify(profile), }); return reply.json(); } No missing await, no missing return. The bug is an assumption I had carried for years: that fetch throws on a 404. It does not. This is the rule that fixes everything once it clicks. fetch rejects its promise only when the network itself fails: DNS resolution failed, the connection dropped, the request was blocked, the host was unreachable. If the server answers at all, the promise resolves, even when the answer is a 404 or a 500. Think of it as two separate questions: Did the server reply? That is what fetch answers. items.title: What I learned building an auto-tiling window manager for macOS with the Accessibility API
items.summary: Snug is a menu bar app that tiles every window the moment it opens. Open a window and it drops into the next free tile; close one and the rest reflow with no holes. There's no config file, and it never asks for Screen Recording permission: it reads each window's position, size and owning app, and nothing else. macOS has no window manager API, so everything goes through the Accessibility API (AXUIElement). Here's what that taught me. Each AX call is a synchronous message to another app, so a busy or hung app can stall the caller. Snug runs one background thread that owns every AX call, every observer and the tiler's state. The main thread only draws UI. A detail worth knowing: a thread's run loop exits immediately if it has no sources, so the AX thread adds a dummy port to keep it alive before any observer exists. RunLoop.current.add(NSMachPort(), forMode: .default) // keeps the run loop alive with no sources There's an AXObserver per running app, listening for window created, moved, resized, minimized and restored, focus changes, and the app hiding or showing. items.title: How to stop duplicate payment callbacks from double-crediting orders (Indonesia QRIS & virtual accounts)
items.summary: A customer pays, the order becomes paid, and your webhook endpoint loses its connection before the acknowledgement reaches the provider. The provider sends the notification again. Nothing unusual has happened to the payment, but your application now has another opportunity to credit the customer. This is the failure sequence I would start with when reviewing a QRIS or virtual account integration. It is a hypothetical example, not a reported production incident. Its value is that every component can behave reasonably while the combined system still produces a duplicate credit. The design question is simple: which durable record prevents a second delivery from causing a second business effect? A webhook delivery is a message about a payment. It is not itself a new payment, and its arrival time does not establish the order of payment events. Keep separate identifiers for the merchant order, provider transaction, and notification event where available. Scope provider identifiers to the integration and merchant account unless the documented contract guarantees a wider uniqueness scope. An event identifier helps detect repeated messages. items.summary: I make small Mac apps you buy once. The newest is MacMuse Recorder, a screen recorder whose main feature is automatic zoom: you click around while recording, and the finished video pushes in on the part that matters. Screen Studio made that look popular. What I wanted on top of it was control: every zoom should be an ordinary block on the timeline, so when the guess is wrong you drag it, retime it or delete it instead of fighting it. This post is how that works under the hood. Everything is Swift on macOS 15+, and the snippets are the real code. While ScreenCaptureKit writes the video, the app keeps three other streams: Cursor samples. Clicks, from an NSEvent global monitor for mouse-down events. Activity. ScreenCaptureKit attaches dirty rects to each frame: the regions that changed since the last one. items.title: Smart Collections Without a Query Engine: Rules That Write Plain Membership Rows
items.summary: Collections in most shops start as hand-picked lists. Someone adds products one by one, and the list goes stale as soon as stock changes or a new product arrives. Smart collections fix that with rules. The interesting part is how we built them, because we deliberately did not build a query engine. A rule is a field, an operator, and a value. The fields are title (contains or equals), tag (is or is not), category (is), price (at least or at most), on sale (yes or no), in stock (yes or no), and new arrival (within 1 to 365 days). A collection matches all of its rules or any of them. Validation rejects an unknown field, an operator the field does not support, a price that is not a number, a category that is not an id, and a new arrival window outside 1 to 365. Those checks run before anything is written, so a bad rule never becomes a collection that silently matches nothing. Because the set is closed, every rule is evaluated in memory against a product's facts: title, tags, category, price, compare-at price, whether any variant is available, and creation time. items.title: Nintendo Is Officially Investing In Game Preservation
items.summary: Nintendo is hiring a digital archivist to help ensure the company's historical records are "preserved for future generations." The 12-month position is tasked with designing and implementing a "structured framework for organizing technical records, engineering documentation, source materials, and institutional knowledge related to legacy systems and platforms." Polygon reports: In the past, Nintendo has drawn criticism from the preservation community. In 2022, the Video Game History Foundation publicly criticized the company for announcing it would be closing the Wii U and 3DS eShops. The foundation released a statement saying that Nintendo's decision was "actively destructive to video game history." The statement also pointed out that Nintendo is part of the Entertainment Software Association, which funds lobbying that prevents a number of preservation efforts. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Two SwiftUI animation loops that burned CPU on my Mac with nothing on screen
items.summary: A looping animation looks free. On macOS, two of mine were not. Both shipped in my own apps, and both were measured on release builds, not Debug. Soluna is my menu bar calendar. Today’s cell had a slow “breathing” glow, a .repeatForever animation on one flag. My own Mac health app, What Happened, reported Soluna using about 134 core-minutes a day in the background. The cause: AppKit keeps an NSPopover’s hosting view alive between opens. So after the popover closed, SwiftUI went on re-rendering its whole view tree every frame. sample showed the main thread in NSHostingView.layout and ViewGraphRootValueUpdater.render with nothing on screen. I proved it by toggling. Open and close the popover: 17 to 19% of a core, and it stays. Close it on a month that does not contain today’s cell: 0.0%. Back to today: 17% again. The rule I took from it: any looping animation inside a popover or panel has to stop when it closes. Wick is my deadline tracker, and a deadline can show a small flame. items.title: Node.js API Error Tracking: Signal Quality for Healthtech Pipelines
items.summary: Short answer: capture one structured error event per failed request, but retain a compact, redacted index longer than the diagnostic payload. In a nightly healthtech pipeline, the bill is usually driven by event count multiplied by retained bytes, not by the act of detecting an exception. Reduce noise at the source: classify failures, fingerprint them deterministically, attach correlation IDs, and keep PHI out of the event. Then make resolution a replayable, auditable workflow rather than a search through unbounded text. Start with the retention equation: retained cost ≈ error events × average event bytes × retention duration That is the whole accounting problem. That equation is deliberately plain. A pipeline that logs every retry, stack trace, request body, and upstream response can create a large searchable archive even when the number of distinct defects is small. The first change should therefore move the dominant term: emit one canonical event for a failed logical operation, and represent subsequent retries as attempts under the same operation ID. items.title: Node.js Kitchen Order Displays: 5 Realtime API Token Contracts
items.summary: TL;DR: Give each kitchen display a read-only, room-scoped token. Let a trusted Node.js service publish compact order transitions to that room, and make every kiosk refetch authoritative state after reconnecting. Choose a managed channel when operating a socket fleet is not part of the product; choose a self-operated fan-out tier when transport control is itself a requirement. For a fintech-operated kitchen order board, delivery guarantees matter more than animation speed. A duplicated order_ready event is irritating; a missed transition can leave a paid order off the pickup screen. The stream is therefore a fast notification path, not the ledger. One event moves the view forward, while one refetch repairs it. This record compares two viable system shapes: a managed room channel and a Node.js-owned socket tier. Both can work. The invariant is stricter than either vendor choice: displays subscribe but never publish, the order service owns transitions, and reconnect always converges from authoritative state. items.title: Next.js 15 App Router: Best Practices I Learned Building 10+ Projects
items.summary: After building over ten production projects with the Next.js App Router, I've accumulated a solid set of patterns that work and an equally long list of mistakes I won't repeat. This post is the article I wish I'd had when I first migrated from the Pages Router. The single biggest mental shift is that components are server-rendered by default. This means you can fetch data directly inside any component without useEffect or client-side loading states. I now fetch data at the component level closest to where it's needed, keeping my pages lean. Only add 'use client' when you genuinely need interactivity — event handlers, hooks, browser APIs. Use fetch() with Next.js cache options for data that changes infrequently Use generateStaticParams for dynamic routes with finite known values Prefer parallel data fetching with Promise.all to avoid waterfall requests Move auth checks into middleware for consistent protection across routes Use React Suspense boundaries to progressively stream content to the client The most common mistake I see is importing server-only modules into client components. items.summary: If you walk into the office of almost any growing wholesale distributor, textile supplier, or regional manufacturer today, you’ll see the exact same setup. A sales rep sits in front of a desktop monitor with two windows open side by side: WhatsApp Web on the left, and a massive, color-coded Excel spreadsheet on the right. Then the messages start coming in: a 40-second voice note or a blurry photo of a handwritten paper slip: "Bro, send 40 cartons of the medium grade like last month, and let me know if charcoal is back in stock." The rep pauses the audio, flips over to Excel, hits Ctrl+F to search the item, and sees stock listed as available. But the warehouse floor hasn't updated the sheet since Tuesday. So the rep calls the warehouse manager, waits on hold for ten minutes, confirms the numbers, and finally texts the buyer back. When you handle five orders a day, this setup feels personal, flexible, and fine. But when you scale to forty orders a day, it turns into a complete profit killer. items.title: Stop Using HasData for All Your Data Seeding in .NET
items.summary: Introduction A fresh database is useless until something fills it. EF Core gives you three different ways to do that, and most projects pick one and force everything through it. That is how you end up with fake data baked into a migration, or a production table that never got its rows. The fix is to stop treating seed data as one thing. In this post I build a small .NET 10 expense tracker on EF Core 10 and SQL Server that uses all three approaches side by side: HasData for fixed reference data, UseSeeding / UseAsyncSeeding for default data the app needs, and a custom seeder class with Bogus for local fake data. One fresh database fills itself with all three, and running the app twice doesn't duplicate a single row. 🎬 Watch the full video here: Three kinds of seed data, three tools Before any code, sort your data into one of these buckets: Fixed reference data - currency codes, country lists. The same in every environment, and it only changes when you decide to change it. Use HasData. Default data the app needs to work, which can grow - the starting categories in an expense tracker. items.title: Your CSV import works on your laptop. Then a customer in Germany uploads a file.
items.summary: A first CSV import often looks like this: const text = await file.text(); const rows = text.trim().split('\n').map((line) => line.split(',')); It works on the Google Sheets export you used for testing. Then a support ticket arrives: "The import says every row is invalid. It's the same spreadsheet we use every month." You open their file: ID;Name;Email;Plan;Seats;MRR;Country C-3001;Jos� Mart�nez;jose@example.es;Pro;6;299,00;ES That one line hides three everyday Excel problems outside the US — and your two-liner hits all of them: Encoding isn't UTF-8 → accented letters become � (file.text() always decodes UTF-8). Delimiter is ; → European Excel uses semicolon when comma is the decimal separator. 299,00 is a number → decimal comma, not "invalid". Add two more traps that show up the same week: newlines inside quoted fields, and dates like 05/03/2025 that mean different days in the US and Europe. Below is how to handle each in the browser with plain TypeScript — no CSV library required. The pattern that keeps support tickets short: validate strictly, suggest generously. items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Reuters: The European Union must rethink security to take into account challenges and risks posed by the growing power of major technology companies that go beyond traditional competition concerns, European Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera said on Monday. "We need to review and to deepen our concept of security, including cybersecurity," Ribera told reporters in Lisbon, arguing that testing and monitoring devices connected to critical infrastructure was no longer sufficient and that security means also ensuring that the Big Tech companies are "governed by democratic and transparent patterns." "We need to be quite quick in the deployment of these new approaches ... This is one of the most critical topics for security, for democracy, and for (our) values," she said. items.title: Mapping every JavaScript call to its ASP.NET endpoint - even in a VB.NET WebForms app
items.summary: Find All References stops where C# ends and JavaScript begins. Here's how I built a Visual Studio extension that links the two - and what legacy code taught me about matching URLs to routes. "If I change this endpoint, what breaks?" On a small ASP.NET Core app you can answer that from memory. On a big one you can't, and Visual Studio won't help you: Find All References stops at the language boundary. It knows every C# call to a controller method, but it has no idea that fetch('/api/orders/checkout') in a JavaScript file, an $.ajax call inside an .aspx page, or an asp-action in a Razor view reaches that same method. I hit this hardest on a legacy application: VB.NET WebForms plus Web API 2, around 780 .vb files, with JavaScript split between a Scripts folder and blocks inside .aspx and .ascx pages. Renaming a route there meant searching for URL fragments and hoping. So I built FullStackCodeLens, a Visual Studio extension that puts a line above your code showing who calls it and where it calls out to - across C#, VB.NET, JavaScript/TypeScript, Razor, Blazor and WebForms. items.title: Blazor Native: HTML and CSS Without a Browser
items.summary: Almost 14 years ago, I had an idea: what if you could build a cross-platform desktop UI with HTML and CSS, but write all of its behavior in C#? At the time, the missing piece was obvious. HTML and CSS are not just convenient ways to describe a UI; they come with a whole ecosystem of parsing, layout, rendering, browser APIs, and edge cases. "Let's just support the useful parts" sounds simple right up until you try to define what useful means. So the idea stayed around, somewhere between "maybe one day" and "that would be a fun project." Then AngleSharp started growing in a direction that made me ask a slightly uncomfortable question: don't we already have the pieces? And isn't Blazor already the C# component model for building UIs? It turns out the answer is: mostly, yes. The result is BlazorSharp, a proof of concept that renders Blazor components into an AngleSharp DOM and paints that DOM in an Avalonia desktop application. No Chromium. No embedded webview. No JavaScript renderer bridge. The components, DOM updates, and rendering pipeline all run in managed .NET code. Let's get the terminology out of the way first. items.title: Sharing private photos with people who will never install your app
items.summary: Our Family Album is a private photo album for families. Parents post a moment once, and the people they invited see it right away. It launched in July 2026. And the main engineering problem turned out to be one sentence I kept hearing from users: "My parents won't install another app." 😅 Version 1.5 added Share without an app. From the invitation screen or an album's menu you can do two things: Create a browser link for one person. It opens the album read-only on any device, with no account. Each link is made for a single person, can expire after 30 days, and can be revoked at any time. Invite someone by email. Each photo email includes a link to the full album, so relatives can catch up from their inbox. Browser access is read-only on purpose. Uploading, commenting and reacting stay inside the app, where people have accounts. The first versions stored some album settings in UserDefaults on the device. That breaks as soon as two family members change settings on two different phones. So now: Album permissions come from the server, not from local storage. A save waits for the server to confirm it. items.summary: Geo Adventures is a geography game: you're dropped into a real street view somewhere in the world, you look for clues, and you pin your guess on a map. It launched in August 2026. It's built with plain UIKit and Auto Layout in code. The challenge was making it not feel like UIKit at all 🎮 Games don't have navigation bars and standard alerts, so I built my own: GameButton: chunky 3D "arcade pill" buttons with a pressed state. GameHeaderView instead of UINavigationBar. GameAlertController instead of UIAlertController. SpringModalTransition for bouncy modal presentations. A starfield background, confetti, Core Haptics patterns and system sounds for feedback. A ThemeManager (the same pattern I use in Email Me) switches between four themes: Midnight, Ocean, Sunset and Daylight. Google Maps SDK shows the Street View panoramas. MapKit handles the guess map and the result map, so those screens don't need a Google key. You can play right away as a guest, even offline. Accounts are optional, and they're built behind a small AuthProvider protocol, with Sign in with Apple and Google Sign-In. items.title: Building a photo booth app that never loses a photo
items.summary: Photo Booth App turns an iPhone or iPad into a self-service photo booth for weddings, parties and company events. Version 1.0 went live in March 2026, and I've shipped more than 20 updates since. An event app doesn't forgive mistakes: if a photo gets lost at a wedding, there's no retake next week. Venue Wi-Fi is usually bad, so the booth never depends on it: Photos and GIFs are captured and saved on the device first. Uploads to the online gallery run in the background and keep going while guests keep using the booth. Finished photos survive the booth restarting or moving on to the next guest. When an event opens, the app checks the gallery and recovers any saved photos that are missing. Sharing by QR code, email or text needs a connection. Taking photos never does. AirPrint is easy to add and hard to get right: A 4×6 template used to print in the corner of a full sheet 🤦 Now the paper size is matched to the template size. Imported artwork snaps to the nearest print size. If it needs more than a small trim, the app tells you how much, and offers to crop, use a custom size, or pick another image. items.title: One photo frame codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple TV, back to iOS 12
items.summary: Digital Photo Frame turns an Apple device into a picture frame. It's been on the App Store since March 2017, and it has shipped more than 160 releases. The interesting engineering isn't the slideshow itself. It's keeping it running, alone, for weeks. The app is one Xcode project with an iOS target, a Mac Catalyst build, a tvOS target and a WidgetKit extension. It's UIKit, with MVVM for the main screens, coordinators for navigation, and a service layer for every photo source: Apple Photos and iCloud shared albums Google Photos Self-hosted servers through Immich or WebDAV/NAS Flickr and Unsplash On the Mac, a small AppKit plugin bundle covers what Catalyst can't do. The deployment target is still iOS 12. A lot of people run the app on an old iPad that can't update anymore, and that's exactly the point of the product. The cost shows up in the dependencies. RevenueCat 5 needs iOS 13, so I vendor a patched copy of RevenueCat 4.43.4 inside the repo instead of pulling it through Swift Package Manager. Not pretty, but it works. items.title: Hour-long voice notes don't fit in an email, so I stopped sending them
items.summary: Email Me does one thing: it sends a note to your own inbox. For years, a voice note was simply an audio file attached to that email. And that worked fine, until people started asking me to record meetings and lectures 😅 Most email providers cap attachments at around 25 MB, and some of them strip or bounce big ones. An hour of speech at the app's old "high" setting (AAC mono at 22 kHz) is about 22 MB. That's already at the limit before any other attachment. On top of that, the recorder had a hard 5-minute cap in AVAudioRecorder, on both iPhone and Apple Watch. A bigger attachment wasn't the answer. The real fix was to separate the audio from the email. So I changed the rule: a recording is a durable file on the server, and the email just tells you about it. The app uploads the audio to the server and gets back a URL. The link can be password-protected. The email carries that link and the transcript, instead of the file. Recordings also stay on the device, in a Core Data library with a full player: waveform, scrubbing and 0.75–2× speed. items.title: Six apps, one developer: how I run an indie iOS portfolio
items.summary: Hey everyone 👋 I'm Manuel, an indie iOS developer from Spain. I build and maintain six apps on the App Store, each with its own website and a small backend. There's no team, it's just me. In this blog I want to share the engineering side: how the apps are built and what broke along the way (spoiler: a lot 😅). All six apps use programmatic UIKit with Auto Layout in code. No storyboards, apart from the launch screens. When I start a new app, I copy the structure of an existing one: Geo Adventures started from Email Me's layout, and Our Family Album from Digital Photo Frame's. So whenever I open any repo, I know exactly where everything is: App/, Configuration/, Controllers/, Models/, Persistence/, Views/. Being the only developer, this saves me a lot of time. RevenueCat for subscriptions and purchases, and Bugsnag for crash reports. A ThemeManager pattern for app themes, reused from app to app. Analytics with one convention in four of the apps: Title Case events, [Screen] Name for screens, and the same base properties on every event. items.title: Swift for Beginners: Build Your First iPhone App
items.summary: Swift is the programming language Apple created for building apps on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. It replaced Objective-C, and today nearly every new iOS app is written in Swift. If you want to build an app for the App Store — or you own an iPhone and want to make something that runs on it — Swift is the language to learn. How does Swift work? You write Swift code in Xcode, Apple's free development tool, and it compiles into a native app that runs directly on Apple devices. Swift is designed to be safe: its type system and optional handling catch many common mistakes before your app ever runs. With SwiftUI, Apple's modern framework, you describe what your interface should look like in code, and the system builds it for you — a text field, a button, and a list can be just a few lines each. You can also use UIKit, the older framework, for apps that need finer control. Swift is a good fit for beginners because it reads almost like plain English. A Swift program is shorter and clearer than the same program in many other languages, and Xcode gives you live previews, so you can see your interface change as you type. items.title: React for Beginners: Build Interactive UIs With Components
items.summary: React is the JavaScript library that powers the user interfaces of Facebook, Instagram, Netflix, and millions of other websites. It was created by Facebook, and it changed how developers build websites: instead of writing pages as one big block of HTML, you build them from small, reusable pieces called components. If you know JavaScript and want to build modern, interactive websites, React is the most useful next step you can take. How does React work? You build your interface from components — a button, a header, a product card — and each component is a JavaScript function that returns what should appear on screen. When your data changes, React updates only the parts of the page that need to change, using its virtual DOM to work out the difference quickly. State holds the data that changes, like what a user typed or which tab is open, and props pass data down from a parent component to its children. That is the whole model: components, state, and props. React is a good fit for beginners because it is just JavaScript with a small set of new ideas. items.title: High-performance .NET: Span , Memory , System.IO.Pipelines, and channel-based concurrency in real services
items.summary: A practitioner's guide to the four .NET primitives that eliminate allocations in hot paths: Span for stack-sliced parsing, Memory for async-compatible slices, System.IO.Pipelines for backpressure-aware streaming, and System.Threading.Channels for producer-consumer concurrency - with a full working service example that combines all four. The profiler says your service is slow. You look at the flame graph and most of the time is in GC collections, not in your actual business logic. That's the signal that you're allocating more than you need to in the hot path. Four primitives address this at different layers: Span for synchronous slices without heap allocation, Memory for the same across async boundaries, System.IO.Pipelines for network-level parsing without double-buffering, and System.Threading.Channels for producer-consumer pipelines without locks. This isn't an overview. I'll assume you know why string.Substring in a tight loop is a problem. The question is how to actually use these in a service under load. items.title: Self-service reporting without hurting your production database: replicas, views, indexes and timeouts
items.summary: By Razi Syed. Sample code: github.com/dotnetreport/dotnetreport You ship self-service reporting, people love it, and three weeks later someone in ops asks why checkout got slow every weekday at 9 a.m. The answer is usually a finance user running "all orders, all time, grouped by customer" against the same database your app writes to, then exporting it to Excel. Twice. Ad hoc reporting changes who writes your queries. Before, every query against production went through code review. Now the person composing a query is a user clicking columns together, and they have no idea which table has 40 million rows. You can't review those queries, so you have to make the environment safe for them instead. This post is the checklist I use, with the specifics of how Dotnet Report (which I work on — disclosure) talks to your database, because you can't tune a workload you don't understand. Most of it applies to any reporting tool, including one you build yourself. items.title: Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?
items.summary: As Hollywood begins to adopt the technology, the professionals in most direct jeopardy are the illustrators mapping out directors’ first visions. They sketch out what could be lost A film industry dominated by AI is a dystopian prospect: stories and dialogue generated by large language models, populated by reincarnated screen icons and uncanny humanoids. That is in the future, but the real-world impact of AI is already directly affecting jobs behind the scenes, as Hollywood’s biggest film-makers begin to adopt the technology. James Cameron – long an advocate for emerging technologies in film-making – is on the board of a gen AI firm, citing his interest in how AI will intersect with CGI; Steven Soderbergh used Meta-powered tech to create animations for his recent documentary about John Lennon; even Christopher Nolan, while dismissing the idea that AI will replace humans as “nonsense”, conceded that it will create some useful “imaging tools”. The current canary in the coalmine however is the storyboard artist, whose work gen AI appears to have directly in its sights. items.title: One app, three native UIs: what I learned building the same app in SwiftUI, WinUI 3 and GTK 4
items.summary: I started this app as "GitHub Lite". All I wanted was a quick way to check my pull requests for new comments, because opening GitHub in the browser made my PC lag so badly that I couldn't work properly. Once that worked, I thought it would be better to automate the next step too, so I built "Fix with agent": it looks at the review comments (it doesn't fix anything itself), writes a prompt from them and starts an agent session to fix them. Then I realized I could do the whole loop inside the app: open the PR, review it, fix, re-request review, answer or leave comments, and so on. Today that app is called PullYard, and it exists three times: a Swift/SwiftUI app for macOS, a C#/WinUI 3 app for Windows, and a Rust/GTK 4 app for Linux. They share no code. Getting the Windows and Linux versions to launch took one day, but that was only launching and minimal functionality. After that I had to work seriously on security and memory leaks, and fix a lot of things. People who hear this tend to ask "why not Electron / Tauri / Flutter?" before anything else. items.title: AppLoggerKit: privacy-first logging for Swift apps (OSLog, JSON Lines, redaction, export)
items.summary: Logs are one of the most common places sensitive data leaks from an iOS app. They end up in sysdiagnoses, support emails, crash tickets and bug trackers, and a single print("\(user)") or "token=\(token)" can put an email address or a bearer token in all of them. I wanted Apple's unified logging, optional log files users can send to support, and real privacy guarantees, without pulling in a third-party SDK. So I built AppLoggerKit: a free, MIT-licensed logging and local diagnostics package for Swift, SwiftUI and UIKit with no third-party dependencies. Module What it gives you AppLoggerCore AppLogger with seven levels, lazy messages, categories and scoped loggers; structured LogRecord with a versioned JSON schema; public / private / sensitive metadata; a Redactor; LogContext for correlation IDs. Foundation only. AppLoggerOSLog os.Logger output with level mapping, Console.app filtering and OSLog privacy annotations. AppLoggerFile JSON Lines files with size/time rotation and retention, streaming search, paging, statistics, and redacted JSON Lines / text / ZIP exports. items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from NBC News: The Food and Drug Administration said Monday that GLP-1 drugmakers must add a warning label about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness. The condition, called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, affects the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain. When blood flow to the nerve is reduced or blocked, it can cause sudden vision loss. The condition is permanent with no known treatment. The FDA said "there is a potential increased risk of rare NAION" in people taking GLP-1 drugs. The agency's requirement applies to all GLP-1s, including Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound, as well as several older GLP-1 diabetes medications. [...] Previous research has found that GLP-1 use may increase the risk of NAION, and Lilly has said it was aware of studies on the potential link. The FDA said it began looking into a possible link after a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology that found diabetes patients prescribed semaglutide were four times as likely to develop NAION as those not prescribed the drug. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions "at the European level." items.title: The datacentre arms race hits pause in south-east Asia
items.summary: Power and water constraints are pressuring what seemed like a juggernaut of growth for the region just months ago In early 2026, Thailand’s datacentre industry was on a roll. The country’s board of investment had recently announced approval of datacentre projects from Tiktok, a UAE-based Skyline datacentre and Singapore’s Bridge datacentres, totalling a planned investment of $27bn. As the year has passed, however, what once seemed like a new industrial juggernaut has ground to a halt. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient details for regulation and monitoring. It is not alone in reconsidering datacentre projects. In neighbouring Indonesia, the governor of the country’s most populous province of West Java halted construction on a datacentre due to lack of permits and an incomplete environmental assessment process. items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity
items.summary: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed ‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.” She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded by Frankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.
